outcomeNote: Migrated: the entry does not state why the re-evaluation fell the way it did.
changedBeliefs: The `Isolate.exit` sacrifice policy (kill the reader to zero-copy a >=256 KB result heap instead of paying the SendPort graph copy) was re-evaluated against the Dart 2.15 isolate-group send model, where SendPort.send SHARES immutable leaves (strings/ints/canonical) and only COPIES the mutable structural graph. Confirmed transport model (`native_vs_heap_send.dart`): send cost tracks the mutable/copyable payload — a heap Uint8List send blows up with size (203-272 us at 512-731 KB) while a native-backed view sends cheaply (23-44 us). So send is cheap exactly when the result is immutable-heavy (text) or externally backed, and expensive only for large mutable structure.

Sacrifice-vs-send crossover (A/B via a reverted RESQLITE_SACRIFICE_THRESHOLD define): on a numeric lane (structure-only, slots = rows x cols) send is faster-or-level up to ~20k slots and sacrifice edges ahead only above ~32k slots by a noisy ~3-4% (2000/8000/20000/32000/48000 slots: sacrifice 76.8/238.6/976.5/1194.8/1856.3 vs send 72.3/226.3/931.9/1233.8/1932.6). On a text lane (200 B strings) send wins everywhere and large (1000 rows: 149.4 vs 438.3 us) because strings are shared on send while sacrifice pays a respawn for a copy it never needed. The crossover metric is STRUCTURAL SLOT COUNT, not bytes.

Neither candidate change survives. Retiring sacrifice (send-always) is rejected because send-always would regress the high-structural-count tail (>= ~32k slots) where sacrifice still wins. Re-triggering on structural slot count instead of estimated bytes is rejected because the crossover sits at a high slot count with a ~3-4% noisy margin and estimated bytes already correlates with slot count for structural results — the accounting complexity isn't paid for. Current 256 KB estimated-byte policy stands unchanged.

Measurement confound identified: within one process the repeated sacrifice respawns accumulate and interfere, so a per-process A/B cannot cleanly isolate a single sacrifice-vs-send at a fixed size — it biases the sacrifice lane by respawn history. This is why the send-vs-sacrifice signal has stayed muddy across exp 241's harnesses (and why the stranded `sacrifice_reeval_ab.dart`, which also lost its `debugReaderSpawnCount` counter to exp 236's cleanup, could not resolve it).
nextSignals: Sacrifice retirement/retuning is REJECTED but not closed. Reopen only with a clean SINGLE-SHOT per-process sacrifice-vs-send harness (one fresh measurement per process, no respawn accumulation) that removes the confound documented here — if that still shows send winning at the high-structural tail (>= ~32k slots), send-always becomes viable. Do not re-run the per-process accumulating A/B expecting a cleaner answer; it structurally can't give one.

A production profile showing real result-size/shape distribution would settle it faster than more microbenchmarks: if results cluster in the send-favored range (text-heavy, or < ~32k structural slots) and sacrifice is firing on the 256 KB byte threshold anyway, that is direct evidence to lower or retire the threshold. The byte threshold is a proxy; the real cost driver is structural slot count of the MUTABLE graph.

General result-transfer-shape rule reinforced: send is cheap for immutable-heavy (shared leaves) and native/external-backed content, expensive only for large mutable structure. Sacrifice pays off only when the mutable structural graph is large enough that the copy exceeds a reader respawn — a narrow, high-slot-count regime, not a general large-result regime.

claims.text: Sacrifice is a state-changing treatment (kills a worker, respawns, clears caches): it cannot be A/B'd in place inside one live pool. Send-vs-exit decomposes into distinct estimands — intrinsic transfer, pool capacity, decode — that must be measured separately.
